title: Packet Routing for the Quantum Internet
abstract: We present a new design for quantum packet routing within the emerging Quantum Internet, highlighting how a little-used feature of Internet Protocol Version 6 (IPv6), namely Extension Headers, can lead to a significant amount of quantumness within the IP layer. Taking a minimalist approach to alterations of established standards, we outline the changes required in order for quantum teleportation, quantum routing, and superpositions of these processes to be enabled. Relative to other proposals for routing within the Quantum Internet, the architecture we propose enables a wider range of outcomes allowed by quantum mechanics. We do not claim any optimally in our design, but rather a pathway to invoke new quantum routing outcomes via small additions to the current IPv6.
summary: This paper proposes a novel architectural modification to the IPv6 protocol stack to facilitate quantum networking functions, such as teleportation and path superposition. By utilizing unused features like Extension Headers, it outlines a pathway for integrating quantum information transfer into existing classical internet infrastructure. The work provides a theoretical blueprint for building the Quantum Internet at the network layer.
main_problem: The core problem is designing a modified Internet Protocol (IP) packet format to enable quantum teleportation, quantum routing (superposition of routes), and superpositions of these processes within the emerging Quantum Internet.
main_result: The authors propose an architecture utilizing IPv6 Extension Headers to incorporate quantum functionality at the network layer, enabling path superposition while maintaining a minimalist approach to standard alterations.
method: The methodology involves adapting the layered structure of the OSI model by proposing new 'Quantum Extension Headers' for IPv6 that carry instructions necessary for quantum operations like teleportation and routing superposition.
model_or_system: The system model is based on modifying the IPv6 packet format (Layer 3) to create a hybrid classical-quantum data stream. It assumes the availability of quantum memory at routers and models information arrival sequentially: classical header first, followed by quantum payload.
key_observables: Quantum teleportation success, path superposition outcomes, and the successful transmission of quantum states via modified IP headers.
important_parameters: The use of IPv6 Extension Headers; the requirement that no router action destroys a requested path superposition (avoiding 'which-way' information leakage).
main_assumptions: Assumes quantum memory is available on all routers, and that information arrives sequentially in pulses (classical header followed by quantum data). The design is explicitly stated as non-optimal.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates a system model demonstrating path superposition using nodes A, B, C, and D. Figure 2 shows the Quantum IP Stack for direct transmission synchronization. Figure 3 proposes the structure of a new IPv6 Extension Header for 'Quantum Routing' to support path superposition.
paper_structure: The paper builds upon existing networking standards by proposing modifications at the IP layer (IPv6). It details the necessary header additions ('Quantum Routing' Header) and outlines how quantum processes like teleportation are scheduled relative to classical control data within this extended stack.
why_interesting: While focused on network protocols, the theoretical framework of encoding complex quantum operations (like superposition) into structured data packets is highly relevant for understanding the physical implementation challenges of distributed quantum computation and communication architectures.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. System Model. A typical system set up where IP routing will be required. Satellite S1 wishes to transmit quantum information to node C via nodes A and B. Here a second satellite S2 sends classical data (header information) synchronized to reach node A just ahead of the quantum information from S1 (systems where S1 also sends the classical information are also possible). Node D may be used, as quantum mechanics allows for a superposition of paths ABC and ADC. The network is assumed perfectly synchronized.

Fig. 2. The Quantum IP Stack. For direct transmission, classical data from the Base IPv6 Header and the Extension Headers are synchronized so that classical data arrives at the next router’s physical layer just prior to the quantum data. The quantum data is then stored in memory whilst the classical data is propagated up through the stack to the IP layer (teleportation involves a different transmission strategy). If the destination address corresponds to that router, the encapsulated TCP/UDP data is propagated to the Transport layer.
